newsitem.title: IRAQ: Saddam warns of deadlock in ties with U.N.
newsitem.headline: Saddam warns of deadlock in ties with U.N.

text.p: President Saddam Hussein said on Thursday Iraq's ties with the United Nations could reach a deadlock if the Security Council did not take measures to lift trade sanctions.

In a three-hour televised address marking the July 17 revolution that brought his ruling Baath party to power 29 years ago, Saddam said Iraq had honoured its obligations and demanded the U.N. to reciprocate.

"As we do not want for the relations between Iraq and the Security Council or between Iraq's representatives and the (U.N.) Special Commission (UNSCOM) to reach a deadlock, we hope that the Council will take measures which could convince us that it has actually started to fulfil its obligations," Saddam said.
UNSCOM, a Security Council affiliate, is entrused with ensuring Iraq complies with the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire resolution by dismantling its weapons of mass destruction.

"Iraq has fulfilled its obligations...It is unacceptable that the Security Council should not acknowledge these sacrifies of Iraq and in turn fulfil its obligations by lifting the embargo...completely," Saddam said in his first address in six months.
UNSCOM must certify that Iraq has no more prohibited weapons before the Security Council can lift curbs on Iraqi oil exports and other trade imposed by the U.N. for Baghdad's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The U.N. has allowed Iraq since December limited oil sales worth $2 billion over six months to buy urgent needs for Iraqis.
Saddam blamed the recent standoff between Baghdad and UNSCOM over arms inspection rights on the United States.

"Because the people of Iraq support their leader and hold on to their rights to sovereignty, the American administration was urging the Security Council last June to adopt a draft resolution to ban Iraqi nationals from traveling abroad," he said.
Iraq's prevention of U.N. inspectors to enter three sensitive sites last month prompted the Security Council to warn Iraq it would face further sanctions if it obstructed inspections.

Referring to the recent Turkish incursion into northern Iraq, Saddam said Turkey would not be able to ensure its security across its southern border without coordinating with Baghdad and ending the mandate of a Turkish-based U.S.-British force which patrols a no-fly zone in northern Iraq.
The force is to protect Iraqi Kurds from possible attacks from Baghdad.

"It (Turkish problem) could be easly solved. First...by the departure of the forces which came under the pretext of 'providing comfort' for the Kurds. Secondly, by coordination among the neighbourly states," Saddam said.
Some 10,000 Turkish troops launched a campaign in to northern Iraq in May against Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) rebels who use bases in the mountains to strike against Turkey.
Saddam criticised Turkey's military pacts with Israel, saying such a rapprochement between them arose "apprehension and suspicion and may lead to hostility" with Arab states.
"We believe that there is a conspiracy against Turkey and against the Arabs with the aim to push Turkish policy to collide with Arab interests," he added.
Commenting on the deadlocked Arab-Isreali peace process Saddam urged Arab countries which have ties with the Jewish state to freeze them and demanded Arabs support the Palestinians.

"All Arabs concerned must freeze their relations with the Zionists if they are not in a position to cancel them at present," he said. "Arab diplomatic efforts should be consolidated to support the uprising of the Palestinian people."
Saddam also suggested an Arab summit to discuss "one subject only, the question of Palestine".
Baghdad newspapers appeared on Thursday with colour portraits of Saddam on the front pages and published articles praising the achievements of the Baathist revolution.
